content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
This paper discusses multi-modal federated learning model, where clients may want to use unlabeled private data. The idea is to use a public proxy labeled data together with unlabeled private data, in a semi-supervised way. The approach has global parameters that are tuned from all clients, and personalized layers to adapt to each client. 

A major concern was the use of public proxy labeled data. Authors suggested that the proxy data may be from a different distribution, but that may lead to generalization issues. Reviewers were also concerned with comparison with relevant work, with some unclear design decisions, and with the design that clients have to share their local embeddings. 

My recommendation to the authors is to first focus on a simpler case, make sure that it is convincing, and only then discuss extensions to multi-modal and mixing of labeled and unlabeled.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: All reviewers recommended reject, and pointed to many issues with the paper. The learning setup is not sufficiently convincing; the writing should be improved; the contribution appears limited in scope; and the experiments are incomplete. The paper is clearly not ready for publication.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors tackle a practical problem of federated learning leveraging multimodal data with limited labels. They propose a method for exchanging multimodal representations between server and clients, namely FedMEKT. They demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed model and show improvement compared to the existing method, MM-FedAvg.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**
- They tackle the practical federated learning with multimodal data
- The results are impressive.

**Weaknesses**
- The critical weakness of the proposed method is leveraging proxy data. In the paper, the explanations of the proxy data are “In terms of the proxy dataset in each dataset, we generate from the subset of data that are separated from training data and testing data, and the size is approximate to the testing data” and “we leverage the small unlabeled proxy data that all clients can access and provide their embedding knowledge
”. According to these, (1) the proxy data is quite artificial. In practical scenarios, how can we get such proxy data which is representative of all clients’ data while not knowing their data modality and distribution? Also, (2) if yet possible, the quality may not be consistent as how to sample them may significantly affect the performance. 

- Another crucial limitation of the method is exchanging the local embeddings. Since federated learning is devised for protection of privacy, sharing not only local data but also any kind of local information (i.e. indirect representation of the local distribution) should not be exposed to anyone. 

- Minor
    - Paper needs to be polished
    - Overview illustration (Fig 1) is hard to understand. Please give a more kind description.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: There are many rooms for improving the quality, clarity and originality of the proposed method.
content.summary_of_the_review: I enjoyed reading the paper, but severe improvement seems to be required, as mentioned above.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a multimodal federated learning model in a semi-supervised learning setting, by essentially adapting autoencoders or classifiers depending on the availability of data for representation learning in a federated learning setup. They propose a model with several modules - global or personalized, and multimodal or classifier (unimodal) networks. Their approach updates the global parameters from the data of each client, and personalized layers to adapt to each client. Experiments on three multimodal human activity recognition tasks show promising results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. The paper is well motivated and described. The ideas are clear and experiments are on several large multimodal datasets.

Weaknesses:
1. My main issue is the lack of reference and comparisons to related work. Starting with https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.01523, the idea of having split global and personalized parameters were used in a federated learning setup to achieve better performance and personalization. https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.01523 also explored personalized autoencoders adaptable to each client before coordinating with a global model. Subsequent work in personalized FL such as https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.07948 and https://openreview.net/forum?id=ehJqJQk9cw are also not referenced and compared to, just to name a few. There should be extensive comparisons to these works since they also operate largely on the local-global split federated learning framework, so it is hard to distinguish the main contribution in this paper.
2. The only comparison is with MM-FedAvg, which is insufficient to capture all the work in personalized FL as mentioned above.
3. There should be more ablation studies on each of the components - importance of global or personalized, and multimodal or classifier (unimodal) networks.
4. Choice of methods is unclear - why should embedding knowledge distillation be used to learn multimodal representations? Why not any of the broader work in multimodal fusion, alignment, or representation learning? See https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03430
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Method seems largely similar to https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.01523 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07078v2, and other works in a huge space exploring the hybrid of both global models and local client models for personalized federated learning. Unclear what the 'multimodal' technical contributions are, and the lack of references and comparisons with crucial related work in both multimodal learning and federated learning.
content.summary_of_the_review: Concerns regarding references and comparisons with crucial related work which limits the empirical claims of the paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a multimodal FL framework with a semi-supervised learning setting, named FedMEKT. A knowledge transfer mechanism is achieved via a multimodal proxy dataset transmitted between clients and the server. The personalized classifier is deployed for each client to improve the local supervised tasks performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Clear training schema and reasonable strategy to deal with the proposed challenges.
2. Nice try on the exploration of the multimodal FL under a semi-supervised learning setting. 

Weakness:
1. The experiment is incomplete. The baseline for comparison is too limited. The original FedAvg, the personalized FL methods, and several existing multimodal federated learning methods are all worth comparing.
2. The writing of the paper is expected to be improved. Especially the methodology part, a more clear and suitable preliminary section will significantly help the reader understand how the method is designed and implemented and realize the unique challenge the method trying to solve.
3. The superiority of the method is doubtable since it can not surpass the only baseline model on several settings while introducing more communication cost.
4. Inconsistent table format. Paper structure and layout are expected to be adjusted.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The methodology part of the paper is not fairly clear. 
The proposed method lacks novelty or is marginally novel since the main idea can be found in previous literature.
The authors provide implementation details for the readers to reproduce their work.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper assumes shared multimodal data on the server side and uses its representations from the global model and local models to achieve knowledge distillation. Basically, this paper adapted the existing methods into the multimodal FL setting from the paper:

Zhao, Yuchen, Payam Barnaghi, and Hamed Haddadi. "Multimodal Federated Learning on IoT Data." 2022 IEEE/ACM Seventh International Conference on Internet-of-Things Design and Implementation (IoTDI). IEEE, 2022.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies the problem of embedding knowledge transfer in muti-modal federated learning setting. Existing multimodal FL work uses the labeled data on the client side. This paper studies a different setting, where a public accessed proxy labeled data, and unlabeled private data, and formulate it in a semi-supervised learning framework. To update the global model, the proposed method leverages knowledge distillation to update the global model by the collaborative embedding knowledge from all clients. The authors compare with the existing multimodal FedAvg method, and show competitive performance. 



--- after rebuttal ---\
Thanks for the authors' response. While it doesn't address all of my concerns. After reading other reviewers' comments, I decided to keep my rating.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength 

-Given the setting that proxy labeled data and unlabeled private data in FL, the proposed embedding knowledge sharing method is technically sound. To handle the multimodal data, the usage of split autoencoder structure is rational. 

-The competitive results are reported compared with the existing baseline MM-FedAvg. 

 

Weakness 

-I have a hard time imagining a practical multimodal FL use case that requires a publicly accessed proxy dataset across clients. Please motivate this problem with practical examples. 

-The method is technically sound. While the major components (e.g. split auto encoder, embedding knowledge transfer) are not new. This limits this paper’s novelty. 

-Figure 1 is hard to follow. It lacks description in both caption and text. 

-The definition of $l_{EKD}$ is missing. Is it l-2 loss or others? 

-In Tables 1 and 2, compared with MM-FedAvg, in several cases (e.g. mHealth), MM-FedAvg shows better performance. The potential explanation is missing. 

-In Table 4, to my understanding, the more rounds of EKT steps towards convergence, the better distillation. It is not clear to me why R=3 is worse than R=2.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper lacks solid motivating examples. Most technical details are clear, despite a few missing definitions or explanations. The major components are not new.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work studies the multimodal FL problem. The reported performance over the existing baseline is encouraging. However, the lack of motivating examples and the limited novelty are my major concern.

content.title: FedMEKT: Split Multimodal Embedding Knowledge Transfer in Federated Learning
content.TL;DR: The paper designs the split embedding knowledge transfer mechanism for multimodal federated learning under semi-supervised learning setting
content.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables a decentralized machine-learning paradigm to collaboratively train a generalized global model without sharing users' private data. However, most existing FL approaches solely utilize single-modal data, thus limiting the systems for exploiting valuable multimodal data in future personalized applications. Furthermore, most FL methods still rely on the labeled data at the client side, which is limited in real-world applications due to the inability of data self-annotation from users. To leverage the representations from different modalities in FL, we propose a novel multimodal FL framework with a semi-supervised learning setting. Specifically, we develop the split multimodal embedding knowledge transfer mechanism in federated learning, namely, FedMEKT, which enables the personalized and generalized multimodal representations exchange between server and clients using a small multimodal proxy dataset. Hence, FedMEKT iteratively updates the generalized encoders from the collaborative embedding knowledge of each client, such as modality-averaging representations. Thereby, a generalized encoder could guide personalized encoders to enhance the generalization abilities of client models; afterward, personalized classifiers could be trained using the proxy labeled data to perform supervised tasks. Through the extensive experiments on three multimodal human activity recognition tasks, we demonstrate that FedMEKT achieves superior performance in both local and global encoder models on linear evaluation and guarantees user privacy for personal data and model parameters.
